entries.narration: Analytics engineering is the work of turning raw data into tables that people can actually trust, and doing it with the habits of software engineering: version control, code review, and tests. dbt is a tool for exactly that work, but it is important to be precise about which part. In an E L T pipeline, something extracts rows from the source systems and loads them, unchanged, into the warehouse. That is an ingestion tool's job, and dbt does not do it. dbt starts from the raw tables that are already there. It owns the T, the transform. You write select statements, and dbt turns each one into a view or a table. Even then, dbt is not the thing crunching the data. It sends SQL to the warehouse, and the warehouse does the heavy lifting. And because dbt never modifies the raw tables, every model it builds can be thrown away and rebuilt from them. So keep three boundaries in mind: dbt is not a loader, it is not a scheduler, and it is not a dashboard. It compiles your SQL, and runs it in the right order. Throughout this course, we follow one small shop: raw orders, payments and customers, becoming staging models, then marts, and eventually a single shared definition of revenue.

When people say dbt, they can mean four different things, and it pays to keep them apart. The engine is the program on your machine. It reads your project files, works out which model depends on which, and compiles everything into plain SQL. The adapter is a plug-in for one specific warehouse. It knows that warehouse's SQL dialect and it holds the connection. Inside Snowflake, the role you connect as decides what dbt is allowed to create. The warehouse, Snowflake in this course, is where the SQL actually executes and where the results are stored. And then there is a hosted platform, which can schedule runs and give you a browser-based editor. It is optional, and nothing in this course depends on it. Versions matter here too. This course pins dbt Core one point twelve, with the matching Snowflake adapter. That is the Python engine, and it is still fully supported. A fresh install now defaults to dbt version two, a rebuilt engine, so wherever the two behave differently, we will say so. Both are open source and free to run on your own machine, and dbt dash dash version prints exactly which engine and adapter you have. To get the same versions as the course, install dbt core and dbt snowflake, both pinned to one point twelve. And whenever something is specific to Snowflake rather than true of dbt in general, it will be labelled.

Before dbt can build anything, it needs two files, and the difference between them is worth getting right on day one. The project file, dbt underscore project dot y m l, says what the project is: its name, where the models live, and default settings for whole folders of them. Folder-level settings carry a plus prefix. Here, everything under staging becomes a view and everything under marts becomes a table. That file is committed and reviewed like any other code. The profile is different. It says how to connect: which account, which user, which role and warehouse, and which database and schema to build into. By default it lives outside the project, in a dot dbt folder in your home directory. A profile can hold several targets, each one a named connection. The dev target here builds into a schema of your own, so your experiments never touch anyone else's tables. Add a second output, say one called c i, and passing dash dash target c i runs exactly the same code into a different schema. That is how one project serves development, testing and production. Notice that the account, the user and the key path all come from environment variables. The credentials themselves never sit in a file that could be committed. Once both files are in place, dbt debug checks that the connection actually works.

A model is simply one select statement in one SQL file. You never write create table or create view yourself. dbt wraps your select in whatever statement is needed. The first model, stg orders, takes the raw orders table and tidies it: it renames columns, casts the date, and lower-cases the status. The second model, fct orders, starts with a config block, which sets behaviour for this one model. Here it asks for a table. A setting in the file wins over the folder default in the project file, and if neither says anything, dbt's own default is a view. Then comes the important part. Instead of naming the staging table directly, fct orders says ref, stg orders. When dbt compiles it, that ref becomes the real relation for whichever target you are running: in dev, analytics dot dbt alice dot stg orders. And ref does a second job. It tells dbt that fct orders depends on stg orders, so the staging model is always built first. That is why you should never hard-code another model's table name. And what does Snowflake finally receive? A create or replace transient table statement, wrapped around your select. Transient tables are the Snowflake adapter's default, which is a Snowflake detail, not a general dbt rule. One honest caveat: stg orders still names its raw table directly. The next course replaces that with a proper source.

dbt has a handful of commands that sound alike but stop at very different points, and confusing them leads to confusing results. Parse reads every file in the project and builds the dependency graph. It does not need a warehouse connection at all. Compile goes one step further and renders all the Jinja, so you can read the exact SQL that would run. You will find it under target slash compiled. Then the work moves to the warehouse. Run executes the models, which means real views and tables get created. Test runs your data tests, which are queries looking for rows that break a rule. Build does all of it, models and tests, plus seeds and snapshots, which come later in the course, and it does them in dependency order. If a test fails, everything downstream of it is skipped rather than built on bad data. When you want to see exactly what happened, look in the target folder. Compiled holds your rendered select statement, and run holds the full statement dbt actually sent, create table and all. One caution. It is tempting to think of compile as completely harmless, but by default it does connect to the warehouse, and some macros run queries while compiling. Compiling is not the same as having no effect on the warehouse at all.

So what did the first build actually give us? Start with the rows. Five raw orders went in, and four came out, because order three was returned and the model filters returns away. The log gives every node a final status: OK, pass, warn, error or skip. The YAML file did two jobs. It described the model and its key column, which dbt docs generate turns into a documentation site, and it attached two tests to order id: unique, and not null. Both passed. Every run also leaves artefacts behind in the target folder. run results dot json records the status and timing of every node, which is the evidence you go back to when something looks wrong. Now, be careful about what this proves. A green build means the SQL ran and the tests passed. It does not mean that excluding returns is the right business definition, and it says nothing about whether every order made it into the raw table in the first place. And every run costs something. A table is rebuilt in full each time it runs, while a view costs nothing until someone queries it. Next, we stop hard-coding raw table names, and declare them properly as sources.

A dbt project is nothing more than a folder of plain text files, and where a file sits tells dbt what it is. There is exactly one project file, dbt underscore project dot y m l, holding the project's name, its paths, and settings for whole folders. Each SQL file under models is one model, a single select statement, named after the file. And alongside them sit properties files, YAML files that carry descriptions, tests and configuration for the resources next to them. The underscore at the start of their names is only a habit, to sort them first. Other folders hold seeds, macros, snapshots and tests, which we meet later, and the target folder is generated on every run, so it never goes into git. Now, the same setting can be made in three places, so you need to know who wins. A folder setting in the project file is the broadest. A config block on the model in a properties file overrides it. And a config call inside the SQL file itself overrides both. We checked this directly: a model set to table by its folder, to view in its YAML, and to ephemeral in its own file, came out ephemeral. The most specific setting wins. The practical advice is to keep defaults in the project file, and make overrides rare, because an override buried in one file is very easy to miss in review.

In the first course, the staging model named its raw table directly: raw dot shop dot orders. That works, but dbt has no idea the table exists. A source fixes that. You declare the raw tables once, in YAML: a source called shop, living in the raw database and the shop schema, with three tables, orders, payments and customers. Then models refer to them by name, with source, shop, orders. When dbt compiles that, it becomes exactly the same raw dot shop dot orders. So what did we gain? The raw table now appears on the dependency graph, so lineage starts at the actual data instead of at your first model. Sources can also carry descriptions, tests and freshness checks, just like models. And if the raw data ever moves to a new schema, you change one line of YAML instead of hunting through every model. But be clear about what a declaration is. dbt never creates a source, and never loads it. That is the ingestion team's job, and if a declared table does not exist, you only find out when Snowflake fails to find it at run time. That is also why the description says who loads the data. Raw data has an owner, and it is usually not you.

Declaring sources also lets you ask whether they are up to date. dbt source freshness asks each source one question: how long ago was the newest row loaded? You tell it which column records the load time, here underscore loaded at, which the ingestion tool writes on every row. dbt takes the maximum of that column and compares it with the current time. Past the warn after threshold, the source warns. Past error after, it errors as stale. In our run, orders were loaded three hours ago and passed. Payments had not been loaded for thirty hours, past the twenty four hour limit, so they errored. Customers were opted out with freshness null, so they were not checked at all. Now the boundary. Freshness tells you that a load happened recently. It does not tell you that the load was complete. A loader that brought in half the rows an hour ago passes with flying colours. And it measures load time, not the business event, so orders placed yesterday can legitimately arrive today. So use the timestamp your loader stamps on each row. A business column like order date measures something else entirely. The habit worth building is to run freshness before a build, so a stale source stops the line instead of quietly feeding old data downstream.

You never tell dbt the order to build things in. It works it out. While parsing, it reads every source call and every ref call, and turns them into a graph: a directed acyclic graph, or DAG. Directed, because each edge points from a parent to a child, and acyclic, because no model may depend on itself, however indirectly. Here are our three raw sources, their three staging models, and the order facts built on top of staging orders. That graph gives you three things. Build order: parents first, and unrelated models in parallel. Lineage: from any raw table to everything built on it. And selection, which a later course uses to build just one model and everything downstream of it. Notice that the two functions resolve differently. A source names a fixed raw table, so it is the same in every target. A ref resolves to wherever that model is built for the current target: your own schema in dev, the production schema in prod. One more rule. Model names must be unique across the whole project. We tried two models called stg orders, in different folders, and dbt refused to compile, because a ref could not know which one you meant.

Sometimes you need a small table that no system produces. Here, the shop records payment methods as codes like credit card and coupon, and the reports want readable labels and a flag for whether it is a card. That is a seed: a CSV file kept in the project. dbt seed loads it into a table in your schema, four rows in our run, and from then on any model can ref it, exactly like a model. Seeds are good for small lookups that people maintain by hand, such as labels, country codes or cost centre mappings, because every change goes through review and its history lives in git. They are the wrong tool for anything an application produces. That is a source, and loading it is ingestion's job. They are also wrong for large or fast-growing data, because every seed run reloads the whole file. And never put personal or sensitive data in a seed, because a CSV in git is copied onto every machine that clones the project. One practical detail: dbt infers each column's type from the CSV, so a code like double-oh-seven would quietly become the number seven. Pin the types with column types in the seed's YAML config. Finally, you rarely need to run dbt seed by itself. dbt build loads seeds too, in dependency order, before the models that use them.

As a project grows, it needs some shape, and the most common shape has three layers. It is worth saying up front that this is a convention, not a feature. dbt does not enforce any of it. Staging comes first: one model per source table, doing nothing but renaming, casting and cleaning. No joins, and usually views, because they are cheap. Our three staging models are exactly that. Intermediate models are reusable steps in the middle, like joining orders to their payments, which we build in the next course. They exist to keep marts simple, and they are not meant for anyone outside the team. Marts are what people actually query: business entities like order facts and customers, documented, tested, and usually tables. Why bother? Because only staging touches the raw sources, raw data has exactly one entry point, and a change upstream is fixed in one place. And consumers see a small, stable set of marts rather than every step along the way. But a folder name proves nothing. Putting a model in marts does not make it correct. The layers organise the work. Tests and review are what earn trust.

One project, many environments. The code does not change between them, the target does. In dev, your target schema is dbt alice. In prod it is prod. Staging models land straight in the target schema. Marts are more interesting, because the marts folder sets a custom schema called marts. And here is the surprise. Plus schema marts does not mean the schema called marts. By default, dbt appends it to the target schema, so marts land in dbt alice underscore marts in dev, and prod underscore marts in prod. We confirmed both from the manifest. If you want plain marts in production, you override that rule with a macro, which we cover in course five. The reason for the default is isolation: if custom schemas ignored the target, every developer would overwrite the same marts. An alias changes the other half of the name. Set alias to orders, and the table in Snowflake is called orders, while every other model still refers to it as ref fct orders. Before you build anything into a shared warehouse, check where it will land. dbt compile or dbt ls will tell you. And look for a generate schema name macro in the project, because many teams override this naming rule, and theirs is the one that applies.

Documentation in dbt lives right next to the code it describes. Models, columns and sources all take a description, and meta holds anything else your team wants to record, such as an owner. dbt does not act on meta. It simply stores it in the manifest, where other tools can read it. dbt docs generate then builds the documentation. It combines the manifest, which holds every description, owner and dependency, with a catalog of actual column types, which it reads from Snowflake. dbt docs serve opens the result as a searchable site with the full lineage graph, from raw sources to marts. And the lineage costs you nothing extra. It is built from the same ref and source calls that order the build, so it can never drift out of date with the code. One more idea belongs here: a source contract. That is an agreement with the team that loads your raw data, covering which tables, which columns, and how fresh they will be. Writing it down in your source descriptions is valuable, but be clear that it is documentation and process. dbt does not enforce it. That is different from the model contracts we meet in course four, which dbt does enforce. The project is now organised and documented. Next, we decide what each model actually means.

Every model has a grain: what one row means. For fct orders, one row means one order, and its key, order id, must be unique at that grain. Grain is easy to break without noticing, and joins are where it usually happens. Order four was paid in two parts, so the payments table has two rows for it. Join orders to payments, and order four now appears twice. Nothing errors. The SQL is perfectly valid. But count the orders and you get five instead of four, and if orders carried an amount of their own, summing it would double order four's value. This is called fan-out, and it is the most common way an analytical model goes quietly wrong. Here, the unique test on order id caught it: it failed with one duplicated key, and dbt build skipped dim customers downstream instead of building it on bad data. The fix is to respect the grain. First aggregate payments to one row per order, in an intermediate model called int order payments, and only then join, so that one order row meets exactly one payment row. It is worth making a habit of this: before writing any join, say the grain of both sides out loud. If they differ, aggregate or pick one row first.

Most marts come in two kinds. A fact records events at a fixed grain, with numbers you can add up. fct orders is one: one row per order, with an amount. A dimension describes things, with attributes you group and filter by. dim customers is one: one row per customer, with their name, their country, and a few summaries such as their order count. The two meet on a shared key, here customer id. Keeping them separate pays off. Facts grow with every new event, while dimensions change slowly, and keeping measures on the fact means they are summed once, at the right grain. Revenue by country, for example, takes amounts from the fact and groups them by the dimension's country. That is a good way to design a mart in the first place: start from the questions people will ask, and find out what they need to filter, group and add up, before writing any SQL. And notice that every mart quietly encodes business decisions. Does a placed order, one not yet paid, count as revenue? Here its amount is zero, so it adds nothing, but someone should decide that deliberately. Whatever the rule is, write it in the model's description, so the next reader does not have to reverse-engineer it from the SQL.

Here is a subtler trap, and it is about time. Most raw tables hold only the current value of each attribute. When something changes, the old value is overwritten. Join old events to those tables, and the old events quietly take on today's attributes. Take an illustrative case. Ana places an order on the first of September, while she lives in the UK. On the twentieth she moves to Germany, and the customers table now says D E. When a report runs in October, joining September's orders through dim customers, her order is filed under Germany. Is that wrong? Not necessarily. If the question is where our customers are now, current values are right. If the question is where we sold last month, you need values as they were at the time of the order. The model has to say which one it gives, in its name or its description. While you are at it, be precise about dates. Order date is when something happened. Loaded at is when it arrived in the warehouse. And time zones can shift both across a day boundary. Until then, name current-state models plainly, and say current in their descriptions. Keeping real history takes snapshots, which arrive in course six.

The same select statement can become very different things in the warehouse, and the materialization decides which. A view stores only the query. It is always current, because every read runs the query again, which also means every read pays for it. That suits staging models, which are light and read mostly by other models. A table stores the rows themselves. Reads are fast, but the data is only as fresh as the last dbt run, and the whole table is rebuilt every time. That suits marts, which many people read. The third option is ephemeral, and it is the odd one out. An ephemeral model creates nothing at all. Instead, dbt pastes its SQL into every model that refs it, as a common table expression with a name starting dbt CTE. You can see exactly that here: int order payments, inlined at the top of fct orders. That keeps the warehouse tidy, which suits small intermediate steps. But there is no relation you can query when debugging, and if several models ref it, each one repeats the work. You can switch materializations freely. Consumers see the same relation name either way, except for ephemeral, which has none.

Everything so far is refreshed when dbt runs, so a table is exactly as fresh as your last scheduled build. Some warehouses can take over that job, and this section is specific to Snowflake. A dynamic table is a table that Snowflake keeps up to date by itself. In dbt you set materialized to dynamic table and give it a target lag, say one hour. dbt creates it once, and from then on Snowflake refreshes it so that it never falls more than an hour behind its inputs. It needs a warehouse for those refreshes, and they cost credits whether or not anyone reads the result. The trade-off is real: freshness stops depending on your scheduler and starts depending on Snowflake's refresh behaviour. Be careful to check what your adapter actually supports. The Snowflake adapter we pinned ships dynamic tables, but it does not implement dbt's materialized view materialization at all; asking for one fails at compile time. Other adapters offer other options, so none of this is portable dbt. A sensible default is to start with tables, and reach for dynamic tables only when a mart must be fresher than your schedule allows.

dbt sends SQL, but the warehouse runs it, so the bill is the warehouse's. What dbt's configuration controls is when you pay, and where. When is mostly the materialization. A table pays at build time, once per run, however many people read it. A view pays at read time, once for every query. A table read a hundred times a day is usually cheaper than the same view. Where is the next question, and here every config is specific to the Snowflake adapter. snowflake warehouse lets one heavy model run on a bigger warehouse while the rest use the profile's default. transient is true by default for tables, which means no Fail-safe period, and cheaper storage, because dbt can always rebuild them. cluster by helps Snowflake skip data in very large tables, and query tag labels each query so you can attribute cost later. Threads matter too. With threads set to four in the profile, dbt runs up to four independent models at once: a faster build, but more concurrent load on the warehouse. Remember that these keys belong to dbt snowflake. Another adapter will ignore them or reject them. And before tuning anything, measure: Snowflake's query history tells you which models actually cost the most.

The moment other people start querying a mart, its shape stops being an internal detail. Its column names, their types, and its grain become an interface, and other people's work depends on them. Some changes are safe. Adding a column breaks nobody. Renaming or dropping a column breaks every query and dashboard that names it, loudly, which is at least easy to notice. Changing a column's type can break things, or worse, get silently cast into something slightly different. And changing the grain is the most dangerous of all, because nothing errors. Turn one row per order into one row per payment, and every dashboard keeps working while its totals quietly change. Ask who will notice. dbt knows about downstream models, because they ref this one. It knows nothing about dashboards or analysts' saved queries unless you declare them, as exposures. So before a breaking change, find the consumers, agree a date with them, and keep the old shape available until then. The next course gives you the tools to make this interface explicit: tests that check it, documentation that describes it, and contracts that dbt enforces.

The quickest checks you can add are generic tests: reusable checks that you attach to a column in YAML, with no SQL to write. dbt ships four of them. Unique and not null together say the key really holds at the model's grain: every order id appears once, and none is missing. Relationships says every customer id in the fact exists in the customers dimension, so no order points at a customer nobody knows about. Accepted values says the status column only contains values from a known list. Under the hood, each test becomes one query that selects the offending rows. dbt test runs them, and dbt build runs each one right after the model it checks, so a failure stops bad data before it spreads. One version detail matters on the release we pinned. Arguments like the list of values, or the model a relationship points to, now go under an arguments key. The older form, with those arguments at the top level, still runs, but it raises a deprecation warning, so write the new form from the start. And remember what these are: data tests. They check the rows that exist today. They say nothing about the rows that arrive tomorrow.

Some rules are too specific to your business for a reusable test. For those, you write a singular test: one SQL file in the tests folder. The convention is simple, and it is worth getting the direction right. The query selects the rows that break the rule. If it returns zero rows, the test passes. If it returns any rows, the test fails, and dbt reports how many. Here, the rule is that no order may have a negative amount, so the query selects orders where the amount is below zero. It refs fct orders like any model, so dbt knows to run it after that model is built. It passed on our data. In fact, every dbt test works exactly this way. A generic test is the same idea written once as a macro, so you can attach it to any column. A singular test is that query written by hand, for one rule. Good candidates are the rules your stakeholders actually care about, like no negative amounts, or revenue never dropping to zero on a weekday. A singular test can also take configuration at the top of its file, such as a severity of warn. Name the file after the rule itself, because the file name is what appears in the log when it fails.

Not every failing row deserves to stop the whole pipeline, and test configuration decides how loudly a test fails. Thresholds are the main tool. warn if greater than zero means any failing row produces a warning. error if greater than five means more than five failing rows produce an error. And severity warn on its own means the test can never error, whatever the count. In our run, one order arrived with a brand new status, refunded. That is one failing row: above zero, but not above five, so the test warned, and the build carried on. The difference matters in a build. A warning is logged, and models downstream still build. An error causes everything downstream of that model to be skipped, rather than built on data that failed its checks. There is one more useful setting: store failures. With it turned on, dbt saves the failing rows to a table in an audit schema named after your target schema, so after the run you can query exactly which values failed. Here, it holds one row: refunded, once. A final word of caution. Warnings are easy to configure and even easier to ignore. A warning that nobody reads is no test at all, so decide who looks at them.

Data tests check the rows that happen to exist. A unit test checks something different: the model's logic, on rows you write yourself. You give it fixed input rows for each model it refs, in place of the real tables, and you state the rows you expect back. dbt runs the model's SQL on those fixtures and compares the result with your expectation. The skill is choosing the inputs. These are the edge cases that matter for fct orders: one ordinary order, one returned order that must be dropped, and one order paid in two parts, whose payments must add up to twelve. On the real model, it passes. Now comment out the line that filters returns, and run it again. It fails with a diff: order three appears in the output, where it should not. That is a logic bug caught before any real data was touched. A few practical details. Because int order payments is ephemeral, it has no table to stand in for, so its fixture has to be given as SQL. In dbt build, unit tests run first, before their model is built. And since they need only fixture data, they are cheap to run on every change, and dbt test with the selector test type unit runs only them.

dbt can see every model that refs another, but its view stops at the edge of the project. The dashboard that reads your mart is invisible to it, unless you declare it. That declaration is called an exposure. It names a consumer, here the revenue dashboard: what type of thing it is, how mature, and who owns it, with a contact. The type can be a dashboard, a notebook, an analysis, a machine learning model, or an application. It also lists what it depends on: order facts and the customers dimension. The exposure then appears in the documentation's lineage graph, at the very end of the chain, which is exactly where consumers belong. That buys you two things. Before you change fct orders, the question of who reads it now has an answer, with an email address attached. And it becomes something you can select: dbt build with plus exposure revenue dashboard rebuilds and tests everything that dashboard reads, and nothing else. Be clear about what an exposure is not. dbt does not connect to the dashboard, and it cannot tell whether the declaration is still accurate. It is documentation in code, so keep it in review, like any other code.

Tests check rows after the fact. A contract works earlier. It declares the shape of a model up front, every column with its type, and dbt refuses to build a model that does not match. You turn it on with contract enforced true. From then on, every column must be listed with a data type, and dbt checks the model's shape before it builds anything. To see it work, we cast the amount column to text. The build stopped immediately, with a table showing the column, the type the model produced, the type the contract promised, and the reason: a data type mismatch. The tests downstream were skipped. Adding or dropping a column fails the same way, because the number of columns is part of the contract too. Contracts can also carry constraints, and here you must know your warehouse, because constraints are enforced by the warehouse, not by dbt. On Snowflake, only not null is enforced. Primary keys, unique keys and foreign keys are recorded as metadata, but Snowflake does not enforce them. So keep your unique and relationship tests. A contract is what makes a breaking change visible, so when the shape really must change, pair it with a new model version, which is next. And be clear about the promise. A contract guarantees names and types. It does not guarantee correct values. A perfectly contracted amount can still be wrong.

Sometimes an interface has to change. Renaming amount to amount total would break every consumer at once, so dbt lets you keep both shapes alive while people move across. These are model versions. Version one keeps amount. Version two renames it. They build side by side, as fct orders underscore v one and underscore v two. A consumer can pin a version explicitly, with ref fct orders, v equals two. A reference without a version resolves to the latest version you declared, here still version one, and dbt warns that it is unpinned, so nobody is surprised when the latest moves. Give version one a deprecation date, and dbt warns at every reference to it, which is a polite but persistent migration reminder. So a migration looks like this: ship version two beside version one, move consumers across, then delete version one and make two the latest. Alongside versions sits access. A model can be private, usable only within its own group, protected, usable anywhere in this project, which is the default, or public, usable from other projects too. One last distinction, and it is important. Access governs which dbt models may ref this one. It is not a permission. Who can actually query the table in Snowflake is decided by grants.

By now fct orders carries data tests, a singular test, a unit test, a contract and an exposure. It is tempting to look at a wall of green checks and feel safe. Instead, ask what each check actually established. Data tests prove that today's rows obey a rule, not tomorrow's. Unit tests prove the logic handles the cases you thought of, not the ones you did not. Contracts prove names and types, not values. Freshness proves a load ran, not that it was complete. And a description states an intent, without proving that the SQL matches it. So test the risks, not the columns. Start from what would actually hurt: wrong revenue, missing orders, amounts in mixed currencies. Then pick the check that covers each risk, and notice which ones no check covers. Write those gaps down. Placed orders counting as zero revenue is an assumption that no test can prove. Put it in the model's description and agree it with the person who owns the number. Next, we look at reusing SQL with Jinja and macros, without hiding what it does.

Every ref you have written so far was already a small piece of Jinja. Jinja is a templating language, and dbt renders it into plain SQL before Snowflake sees anything at all. There are three kinds of tag. Double curly braces are an expression: whatever value is inside gets printed into the SQL, such as the relation a ref resolves to, or the current target's name. Curly brace and percent sign is a statement, such as set, if or for. A statement controls what gets written, but prints nothing itself. And curly brace and hash is a comment, which is removed entirely. Here is the part that explains most Jinja surprises in dbt. Every model is rendered twice. First at parse time, when dbt only wants to find every ref and source to build the graph. At that point a variable called execute is false, and there is no database connection. Then again at compile time, to write the final SQL, with execute set to true. So anything in a model that queries the database has to cope with both renders. Inside those tags, Jinja can read ref and source, the current target, project variables, environment variables, the relation being built, called this, and every macro in your project and its packages. And remember, Snowflake never sees any Jinja. When the result looks wrong, read the compiled SQL in the target folder first, because that is the code that actually ran.

Here is a common job: one column per payment method, each a sum of that method's amounts. Writing four nearly identical sum case lines by hand is tedious, and it invites a typo in exactly one of them. A loop writes them for you. A set statement holds the list of methods. A for loop repeats a block of SQL once per method, and the method's name is printed into both the condition and the column name. loop dot last lets you drop the comma after the final column. Compile it, and the loop has unrolled into four plain columns, and the result is a pivot: order four paid five in bank transfer and seven in gift card. Values can also come from outside the model. var reads a project variable, with a default, which you can override on the command line with dash dash vars. env var reads an environment variable, just as the profile did with credentials. And an if on target dot name can, for example, limit development builds to recent data. One warning. Jinja builds a string of text. It does not understand SQL at all, so a missing comma only fails later, when Snowflake runs the result. That is why reading the compiled file is a habit worth keeping.

A macro is a reusable piece of Jinja with arguments, saved in the macros folder, and called like a function. Here is a small one. cents to dollars takes a column name and an optional scale, and returns the rounded division. Arguments can have defaults, so passing four keeps four decimal places instead, and a macro can also return a value rather than printing SQL. Every model that converts cents now calls the same macro, so the rule lives in exactly one place, and stg payments compiles to round amount divided by one hundred, two. Now a more powerful idea. Much of dbt's own behaviour is written as macros, and you can replace them. In course two, custom schemas were always prefixed with the target schema, so prod built into prod underscore marts. Define a macro called generate schema name in your project, and dbt uses yours instead. This one keeps the prefix in development, so developers stay isolated, but in production uses the custom schema exactly as written, plain marts. We checked both targets: dev still lands in dbt alice marts, and prod now lands in marts. A word on restraint. Every macro hides some SQL from whoever reads the model. Reach for one when the same logic repeats in three or more places, and keep it small enough to understand at a glance.

The dependency graph comes from the ref calls dbt meets while parsing. That sounds airtight, but there is a gap: a ref that parsing never reaches is never recorded. The commonest way to hide one is to put it inside an if execute block. At parse time, execute is false, so the whole block is skipped, and the ref inside it is never seen. A missing edge matters in two ways: it breaks build order, and it hides the model from graph selections like stg orders plus. Here, a model counts the orders in stg orders with a query inside exactly such a block. Parsing records no dependency at all. Then, at compile time, the block runs, the ref is finally evaluated, and dbt stops with an error. It says it was unable to infer all dependencies for the model, because it cannot be sure stg orders was built first. Helpfully, the error tells you the fix. Add a depends on hint as the first line: a SQL comment containing the ref. Snowflake ignores the comment, but dbt's parser still reads the ref inside it, so the edge is recorded, and the model builds in the right order. The better lesson, though, is to keep ref calls plain and at the top level of a model, where every reader, and dbt, can see them.

A package is simply someone else's dbt project, installed into yours so that you can call its macros, tests and models. The best known is dbt utils, with helpers for surrogate keys, date spines and extra generic tests. Using one takes three steps. First, packages dot y m l names each package, either from the dbt package hub with a version range, or straight from git with a revision. Second, dbt deps downloads them into a dbt packages folder. Third, dbt deps writes a lock file. We installed dbt utils at tag one point three point zero, and the lock records the exact commit that tag pointed to, along with a hash of the whole specification. Commit that lock file. With it, every developer's machine and every CI run installs exactly the same code. Without it, a version range can quietly resolve to a newer release tomorrow, and a build changes without anyone changing the project. To upgrade on purpose, change the range or revision and run dbt deps with dash dash upgrade, which rewrites the lock, and review that diff like code. The installed dbt packages folder itself stays out of git. Finally, think about provenance. A package's macros run with your warehouse role, and can do anything your role can do. Read what you install, prefer well-maintained packages, and pin them.

SQL dialects differ between warehouses, and sometimes a macro has to produce different SQL depending on where it runs. dispatch is dbt's answer. The outer macro, day bucket, does nothing except call adapter dot dispatch with its own name. dbt then looks for an implementation named for the current adapter, here snowflake underscore underscore day bucket when running on the Snowflake adapter. If there is none, it falls back to the default underscore underscore version. A dispatch entry in the project file controls which namespaces are searched, and in what order. We compiled the same model on both adapters. On Snowflake, it became to date of ordered at. On another adapter, it became date trunc day. One macro name, one model, two dialects. You will mostly meet dispatch inside packages. dbt utils dispatches internally, which is how a single package works across many warehouses, and dbt lets you override a package's implementation for your adapter from inside your own project, when you need to. If your project only ever runs on Snowflake, you will rarely need to write a dispatched macro yourself. But knowing the pattern explains why the same package call can compile to different SQL in different projects.

Some Jinja does more than write SQL. It runs SQL, and you need to know when, and how often. run query executes a query while the model is being compiled. Our example counted the rows in stg orders at compile time. The answer, six, was frozen into the compiled SQL as a plain number. So compiling that model did real database work, and the number will be stale the moment new orders arrive. Hooks are another way. A pre hook or post hook runs statements just before or after one model. on run start and on run end run once per invocation, which suits audit rows and housekeeping. And dbt run operation calls one macro on demand, outside any build. We used it to log the order count. Inside a hook, this refers to the model's own relation. And hooks run on every single build, so write them to be safe to repeat. Now, the execute guard. Wrapping a query in if execute stops it from running at parse time, when there is no connection. It does not stop it anywhere else. At compile, run and build, it still runs. One practical recommendation: for granting access, use the grants config rather than a post hook. dbt then knows which grants should exist, and applies them consistently.

A model does not have to be SQL. It can be a Python file, and on Snowflake it runs through Snowpark, inside the warehouse, not on your laptop. The shape is fixed. You define a function called model that takes dbt and a session, and returns a DataFrame. dbt dot ref and dbt dot config take the place of Jinja, and you can ask Snowflake for libraries it provides, such as pandas. This one computes, for each customer, the number of days since their previous order, which is awkward to express in SQL but simple in pandas. There are firm boundaries. On the Snowflake adapter we pinned, Python models can only be materialized as tables or incremental models. There is no Jinja, so no macros inside the model. And each run starts a Snowpark session and spends warehouse credits. The model shown here parses, and dbt records fct orders as its parent, but it needs a Snowflake account to run. Use Python where SQL is genuinely awkward. For joins and aggregation, SQL stays clearer, and usually cheaper. Next, we stop rebuilding tables from scratch, with incremental models.

Every table so far was rebuilt from scratch on every run. That is simple and safe, but as payments pile up, rebuilding years of history every hour gets slow and expensive. An incremental model builds everything once, and afterwards only processes what is new. The switch is a macro called is incremental, and it is true only when three things hold: the model is materialized as incremental, its table already exists in the warehouse, and the run is not a full refresh. That means one file compiles in two different ways. On the first run, or whenever you pass dash dash full refresh, the filter disappears, and dbt creates the whole table from the full select. On later runs, the filter applies, so only payments newer than the newest one already in the table are selected, and dbt merges them in, matching on the unique key. We ran it, and the two compiled files show exactly those two paths. On the second day, the run read one new payment instead of all of them, so the cost grows with what changed, not with the size of the history. Here is the rule that keeps incremental models safe. The full-rebuild path must stay correct. Every incremental run is just an optimisation of that rebuild, and should end up with exactly the same rows.

The incremental filter works by comparing incoming rows with a watermark: the newest value already in the table, here the maximum paid at. On the happy path it works perfectly. On day one, the first run builds payments one to three: three rows, thirty five in total, matching the source exactly. On day two, payment four arrives, the filter reads only rows paid after the current maximum, and the table now holds four rows and forty two, still matching. But choosing the watermark column is a real decision. paid at is when the payment happened. A payment can arrive in the warehouse days later, still carrying its older paid at time. underscore loaded at is when the row arrived, which only ever grows, so nothing can slip in behind it. Often the best answer is both: filter on loaded at, and keep paid at for reporting. The reason this matters is that the boundary is permanent. A row that lands on the wrong side of the watermark is never read again by any incremental run, and nothing errors to tell you. So for every incremental filter, ask one question: what happens if a row arrives late? The next sections answer it with a real late payment.

Once new rows are selected, something has to combine them with the table that is already there. That is the incremental strategy, and this list is specific to the Snowflake adapter we pinned. Merge is the default. Rows whose unique key already exists in the table are updated, and the rest are inserted. Delete plus insert gets a similar result another way: it deletes the matching keys first, then inserts everything. Append does no matching at all. It is fast, but anything read twice is stored twice. Two strategies deserve a careful read. Microbatch rebuilds whole time batches, one day at a time for example, and it needs an event time configured on its inputs too; without that, dbt warns that it cannot filter them and may produce duplicates. And insert overwrite on Snowflake replaces the entire table, not a single partition, which is very different from what the same name does on other warehouses. Finally, be precise about unique key. It is a rule for matching rows during a merge. It is not a test and it is not a constraint. It never checks that keys are actually unique, so add a unique test for that.

Here is the late row. Payment five happened on the second of September, but only arrived in the warehouse on the fourth, by which time the table already held payments from the third. The original filter, paid at greater than the maximum, never saw it. After the run, the table held four rows totalling forty two, while the source held five totalling forty five. And the run reported OK. Nothing failed. The fix is a lookback window. Instead of strictly newer than the maximum, read everything from three days before it. With merge on the unique key, the run picked up payment five, re-read a few rows it already had, merged them harmlessly, and ended with five rows and forty five, matching the source. We also tried the same lookback with append. Every re-read row was inserted a second time: ten rows, ninety in total, double the truth. How long should the lookback be? Measure it. Compare loaded at with paid at across your history, set the window past the worst delay you are willing to accept, and rebuild every so often to catch anything later still. So the pattern is a lookback long enough to cover how late your data really arrives, paired with a unique key so that re-reading is safe. That only works if the same row comes back the same each time, so deduplicate the source in staging first.

An incremental table outlives many versions of the SQL that builds it, so changes to its columns, and deletions upstream, need a plan. We added a currency column to the payments model. With on schema change left at its default, ignore, the new column was simply left out of the table. No error, no warning, just missing. With append new columns, the column appeared in the table, but look at which rows have a value. Only the rows that this run happened to re-read through its lookback window got a currency. Everything older is null. on schema change changes the table's shape; it never backfills history. Deletes are the other gap. We deleted payment two at the source. An incremental run only reads recent rows, so it never noticed, and payment two is still in the table, contributing to every total. Neither problem fixes itself. To fill a new column for every row, run a full refresh. For deletes, handle them explicitly, for example with a soft-delete flag from the source that the model can filter on, or with a periodic full rebuild.

Incremental tables drift silently, so you need a way to find the drift, and a way to repair it. Reconciliation finds it. Compare simple counts and totals between the table and its source. After the late payment, the table held four rows and forty two, while the source held five and forty five. A query like this one can live in the analyses folder, which dbt compiles, resolving every ref, but never runs, so you run the compiled SQL yourself, or turn it into a singular test. Repairing is usually a full refresh. dbt run, selecting fct payments, with dash dash full refresh, ignores the existing table and rebuilds it from the source. Ours came back with five rows and forty five. When a table is too big to rebuild, backfill a window instead: give the model's filter a variable for its start date, and pass that variable on the command line. One warning before you reach for a full refresh. It rebuilds from whatever the source holds today. If the source has already deleted old rows, the rebuild loses them. So check the source's retention before you rebuild.

Course three left a gap. The raw customers table keeps only today's country, so history is lost the moment it changes. A snapshot keeps it. Every time it runs, a snapshot compares the source with the latest version it already holds. When a row has changed, it closes the old version by setting dbt valid to, and opens a new version with dbt valid from. We ran it twice, with Ana moving from the UK to Germany in between. The snapshot now holds a UK row that ends at the second run, and a current row for Germany, while Ben and Chi each have a single current row. There are two ways to detect a change. The timestamp strategy trusts an updated at column on the source. The check strategy compares the values of chosen columns directly, which we used here because the raw table has no updated at column. Be careful with the dates. dbt valid from records when the snapshot noticed the change, not when Ana actually moved. Snapshots are defined in YAML, and run with dbt snapshot, or as part of dbt build.

A snapshot records what each run observes. Between runs, it is blind. Ben moved to France and then back to the UK between two snapshot runs. The second run saw UK, exactly as before, so the snapshot holds no trace that France ever happened. If short-lived changes matter to you, the only answer is to run the snapshot more often, or to get change history from the source itself. Deleted rows need a decision too. Dev was deleted from the source, and the hard deletes setting decides what the snapshot does. With ignore, the default, Dev simply stays current forever, as if he still existed. With invalidate, his row is closed, so he drops out of current views. With new record, the snapshot adds a fresh row marked as deleted, which keeps the deletion itself as part of the history. We ran the last two and saw exactly that. Also, snapshot raw sources rather than marts. A mart's logic changes over time, and its history would mix old and new definitions, while the source's facts do not. Finally, treat a snapshot as source data, not as a model. It holds history that exists nowhere else, so a rebuild cannot recover it. Never drop it or full-refresh it, and make sure it is backed up. Next, we look at choosing exactly what to run.

Most commands do not need the whole project. The select flag, dash s, chooses what a command touches, and because dbt knows the DAG, the choices can be precise. A plus after a name means the model and everything downstream of it. stg orders plus selects stg orders, fct orders and dim customers. A plus before the name means everything upstream: plus fct orders selects it and the three models it is built from. A number limits the depth, so one plus fct orders goes up a single generation. And the at sign selects a model's descendants plus everything those descendants need, which here turns out to be all six models, because dim customers also needs the customers staging model. Selections combine like sets. A space between two selectors is a union, and a comma is an intersection: stg orders plus, comma, marts, gives only the downstream models that live in the marts folder. dash dash exclude removes nodes from the result. Selections you use often deserve a name: a YAML selector, with a description, reviewed like code. And before you run anything, dbt ls shows exactly what your selection selects.

When you select a model, its tests come along without being named. Which tests, exactly, is decided by a setting called indirect selection. Select fct orders with the default, eager, and you get every test that touches it, including the relationship test that also points at dim customers, even though dim customers itself was not selected. Switch to cautious, and dbt only includes tests whose every parent is selected, so the relationship test is left out. We checked both with dbt ls. There are two more settings, buildable and empty, for the cases in between. You can also narrow a selection by kind of test, with test type unit, or test type data. Ordering inside dbt build follows the graph. A model builds once its parents have succeeded, its tests run right after it, and only then do its children build. When something errors, everything downstream is skipped. We introduced one typo in stg payments, and the build reported one error and seven skipped nodes: the payment models, order facts, customers, and their tests. Remember the boundary of a partial build, too. A green result for the nodes you selected says nothing at all about the ones you did not.

Every dbt invocation writes JSON files into the target folder, and they are your evidence about what happened. Four matter most. The manifest is the whole project as parsed: every node, its configuration, and every dependency. Run results records what this particular run did, node by node, with a status and timing for each, and on Snowflake, the adapter adds the query id and the number of rows affected. The catalog holds the actual column types, read from Snowflake by dbt docs generate. And sources dot json holds freshness results. Each one is evidence about one thing, so be careful about what it cannot tell you. The manifest describes the code, not the warehouse. A model can appear in the manifest and never have been built, or have been built last week from older code. Run results describes this run only, and says nothing about earlier ones. And here is a practical trap. The next run overwrites the target folder. Any artefact you will need later, such as the manifest from your last production run, has to be copied somewhere safe. The next section depends on exactly that.

Once you have a saved manifest from production, dbt can compare your current project with it and select only what changed. That is state colon modified. We saved a production manifest, then changed just one thing: the cents to dollars macro now keeps three decimal places instead of two. No model file was touched. Even so, state modified selected stg payments, because it calls that macro, so its compiled SQL changed. Adding a plus, state modified plus, brought in everything downstream of it as well: the intermediate model, the payment facts, the order facts and customers. Everything else was left alone. That is the foundation of efficient CI, which we use in the next course. To make it work, save production's manifest after every production run, in a folder of its own, separate from the target folder that each run overwrites, and point dash dash state at it. And remember what is being compared: two manifests, which describe code. State comparison knows nothing about data. A model whose code has not changed can still be wrong, or stale, in the warehouse.

Say you changed fct orders and want to build just that model, without first rebuilding everything upstream into your own schema. Its parents already exist in production. dash dash defer, with a saved production manifest, lets you use them. The rule for each ref is this. A model you selected is built in your own schema, as usual. A parent you did not select, and which does not exist in your dev schema, resolves to production's relation, taken from the state manifest. But a parent that does exist in your dev schema is used from dev, unless you add dash dash favor state, which prefers production even then. Combined with state comparison, this is what makes CI cheap: build only what changed, and read everything else from production. We ran exactly this, and the compiled SQL shows the consequence. The one model read stg orders from production, because it had never been built in dev, and stg payments from dev, because an old copy was lying around from an earlier experiment. Two environments, mixed into one result. So before trusting a deferred build, remember that deferral does not check that production is fresh, or that production was built from the same code as yours. Read the compiled SQL to see which relation every ref actually used.

Threads decide how many nodes dbt runs at the same time. You set them in the profile, or with dash dash threads on the command line. With four threads, independent models start together, and you can see it in the log: they finish out of numeric order, the seed first, then staging payments, customers and orders. Our profile sets four, and dash dash threads one makes a run much easier to follow when debugging. What threads cannot do is speed up a long chain of dependencies. Each step still waits for its parent. It helps to know where the time actually goes. dbt itself parses and compiles, usually in seconds. Then each query may wait in a queue, until the warehouse has room to accept it. Then Snowflake executes it. More threads is not free. Every thread is another concurrent query against the same warehouse. If the warehouse is already busy, extra threads simply queue, and teams then reach for a larger warehouse and a larger bill. So measure before changing anything, and remember that the execution time dbt reports for a model includes any time it spent queueing.

This model is slow is a claim, and you can follow the evidence for it from dbt into Snowflake. Start with dbt's own artefacts. Execution time in run results tells you which node took how long. The compiled folder holds your select statement, rendered. The run folder holds the full statement dbt actually sent, including the merge or create table wrapped around your select, which is often where the surprise is. Then move into Snowflake. The Snowflake adapter records each query's id in run results, so you can find exactly that query in Snowflake's query history, or you can search by the query tag you configured in course three. Open its query profile, and Snowflake shows where the time went: how many bytes were scanned, whether it spilled to disk, how long it waited in the queue. Only then decide what to change. A full table scan on a large table suggests a better filter, or clustering. Rebuilding years of history every run suggests an incremental model. And a long queue time suggests a scheduling problem, not a SQL problem at all.

When a build fails halfway, the project is left partly built. Some nodes were rebuilt, some were skipped, and some were never touched. Here, a typo in stg payments produced one error and seven skipped nodes, while three nodes succeeded. After fixing the typo, there is no need to rebuild everything. dbt retry re-ran exactly the eight nodes that errored or were skipped, not all eleven, and they all succeeded. Retry knows what to re-run because it reads the run results file from the previous invocation. That has a consequence. If you run any other dbt command in between, even a quick dbt ls, that file is replaced, and retry is working from the wrong run. Be clear, too, about what retry does not do. It does not undo the three nodes that already succeeded, and it does not check whether their inputs have changed since. Finally, retry, state comparison and deferral are behaviours of a particular engine and version. Check them on the one you run, especially if you move to dbt version two. Next, we take all of this into reviewed, deployed production work.

Every change to production should travel the same path. You work on a branch, building into your own development schema. You open a pull request. A CI job builds and tests the change in a schema of its own. A reviewer approves it, it merges into main, and a scheduled production job, running as a service identity, picks it up. This works well for dbt because a dbt project is just text: SQL, YAML and Jinja. Git versions every line of it, and a pull request shows exactly what changed. A good reviewer reads more than the SQL diff. They ask whether the grain of a model changed, which no diff announces. They read the YAML diff, for tests, contracts and owners. For macro-heavy models, they read the compiled SQL, because that is what will actually run. And they read the CI result, including what it skipped or did not select. Ownership makes review real. Owners recorded in each model's meta, and a code owners file in the repository, decide who must approve a change to a given mart. Keep pull requests small, too: one model or one concern each, so a reviewer can hold its grain in their head, and a revert is clean. And the rule underneath all of it: nobody edits production by hand. Main is what runs.

CI needs somewhere to build that is neither your schema nor production's. The usual answer is one schema per pull request. The profile gets a CI output, with its own user, its own key and its own role, so CI can never write where production lives. Its schema comes from an environment variable, so pull request one two three builds into ci pr one two three, and custom schemas follow the same prefix, giving ci pr one two three underscore marts. Those schemas must be cleaned up when the pull request closes, and our first attempt taught a lesson. Dropping only the target schema left the marts schema and the test audit schema behind, because each custom schema is a separate schema. So the cleanup macro lists every schema in the database and drops the ones that carry this pull request's prefix, carefully, so that cleaning up pull request one two three never touches one two three four. It also refuses to run on any target that is not CI. Development schemas pile up the same way, full of models nobody has built for months, so sweep those on a schedule too. Why bother? Stale CI schemas cost storage, and they confuse anyone browsing the warehouse for the real tables.

Rebuilding the whole project for every pull request gets slow and expensive as the project grows. Slim CI builds only what the change touches, and it combines two ideas from course seven. state modified plus selects what changed and everything downstream of it. And defer, with production's saved state, reads every other parent from production, instead of rebuilding it. Pull request one two three changed only stg orders. CI built three models and four tests in its own schema, and read everything else, like stg payments, from production. Much depends on where that saved manifest came from. It has to be the manifest of the latest production run. If it is stale, state comparison selects the wrong set of changes, and deferral reads from relations built from older code. So publish the production manifest as part of every production run, and have CI fetch exactly that. Finally, be precise about what a green Slim CI run means. The change compiles, builds and passes its tests on today's data, against production's parents. It does not mean production is fresh, and it says nothing about performance at production scale.

Each environment should run as its own identity, with only the access that environment needs. On Snowflake, that means separate roles. A developer's role can write only their own development schemas. CI's role can write only the pull request schemas. The production job's role writes production. And dashboards use a reporting role that can only read marts, never raw data and never staging. Secrets follow the same discipline. They never live in the repository. The profile reads them with env var, and your secret manager fills those variables at run time. Key-pair authentication with one key per identity means a single identity can be revoked without disturbing the others. Grants belong in code too. Setting grants, select to reporter, on the marts folder means dbt applies that grant every time it builds a mart, so access never silently disappears after a rebuild. One last rule is easy to break by accident. A person's own login should never run production, because when that person leaves the company, production should not leave with them.

dbt does not schedule itself. Something else runs it, an orchestrator, and the order of the steps matters more than the tool. A sound production job does four things in order. First, it waits until ingestion reports that its load has finished. Second, it runs dbt source freshness, and stops if a source is stale, rather than publishing yesterday's numbers as today's. Third, it runs dbt build. Fourth, it keeps the manifest and the sources file, because the next run, and CI, will need them. That saved sources file enables a useful selector. source status fresher plus compares source freshness with the previous run, and selects only what new data actually touched. In our run, new payments had arrived but orders had not, so dbt selected staging payments and its four descendants, and left orders alone. Finally, a schedule is not a dependency. Run at six o'clock quietly assumes the loader finished by five fifty nine. When it is late, the job builds on stale data. Trigger the job on the load finishing where you can, and keep freshness checks as the safety net.

Some changes can ship in a single release, and some cannot. Compatible changes, like adding a column or adding a new model, break nobody, so you merge and deploy. Breaking changes need several releases, in the right order. Take renaming amount in fct orders. Release one adds version two beside version one, both contracted, so consumers can start testing against the new shape while nothing breaks. Then comes the handoff. You tell the owners listed in your exposures, and agree a date. In release two, consumers pin version two. In release three, after the deprecation date, you delete version one. Ordering matters inside the project too. A model has to deploy before, or together with, the models that read it, never after them; otherwise the downstream model fails, or reads a shape that does not exist yet. Before merging any release, dbt ls with state modified plus lists every model it touches, which is the list to check. And notice that the handoff in the middle is a conversation, not a deploy. dbt can remind you, with deprecation warnings at every reference, but it cannot agree a date with the finance team on your behalf.

Production dbt has to run somewhere, and there are two broad options. The first is your own orchestrator, such as Airflow, Dagster, a CI runner, or even cron, calling the dbt command line. You then own the plumbing: storing the production manifest for state comparison, wiring retries, and managing secrets. The software is free, but you pay in engineering time. The second is a hosted dbt platform, which runs dbt for you, with scheduling, a browser-based editor, stored state and run history built in. It costs a subscription, and its features vary by plan and by engine, so check the eligibility of any specific feature before you depend on it. How to choose? If you already orchestrate ingestion, adding dbt to that same DAG lets one step wait on the other naturally. A small team starting fresh may value the hosted plumbing more. Some things do not change with the choice. The project is the same repository and the same DAG. The warehouse still does the work, and still sends the bill. And waiting for ingestion is still your responsibility to wire up, whichever tool runs dbt. Everything in this course runs with the free command line and no hosted service at all.

There are two ways to depend on dbt work done by someone else, and they are easy to confuse. A package is someone's code, installed into your project and built inside it, pinned by the lock file, as in course five. Depending on another project is different. You want its published models, built and owned by that team, referenced as ref finance, fct invoices. In dbt Core one point twelve, that does not work on its own. dbt deps ignores a projects entry in dependencies dot y m l, and the reference fails with not found. Resolving another project's published models is a capability of a hosted platform, so check its eligibility for your plan. Some boundaries hold either way. Access set to public, together with a contract, marks exactly what other teams may build on. Groups and owners say who answers for each model. And one governance setting is worth knowing about: dbt Core sends anonymous usage statistics by default, and a project flag, send anonymous usage stats false, turns that off if your policy requires it. Next, we look at keeping all of this running.

A green run tells you the SQL ran. Production needs signals that would actually catch the failures that matter, and there are four worth having. Run status, from run results: did every node succeed? Freshness, from the sources file: is the data recent? Data tests: do the rows obey the rules you wrote down? And consumer health: does the mart match what its users mean by it? That last one is the one teams skip, and here is why it matters. A new order, order six, arrived with the status refunded. The accepted values test only warned, every other test passed, and the mart reported revenue of fifty nine. But finance counts revenue only for completed and shipped orders, which comes to twenty five. The difference is the refunded order and an unpaid placed order. Nothing in the pipeline was broken. The mart simply disagreed with its consumer. The fix starts with a conversation, to agree the definition, and ends with encoding it: a singular test using finance's own rule failed immediately, and it now runs in every production build. And route alerts to the owner of the model, not to a shared channel that nobody reads.

Here is a typical failure. Both staging models built successfully. Then fct orders failed, with an error saying it could not convert the string completed to an integer. Diagnose it in a fixed order. Start with the console, then the log file, logs slash dbt dot log, which records every query dbt ran, at debug level, including the full error. Then open the run folder, which holds the exact statement dbt sent to the warehouse. Then run that statement yourself in Snowflake, using the job's role rather than your own, because permissions often differ. Before fixing anything, ask what the warehouse holds right now. The staging views were rebuilt by this run. fct orders still holds its previous version, intact, because a failed table build does not replace the table that was already there. And dim customers was never reached, so it is as old as the last successful run. Only then fix the cause, here a cast applied to a text column. Fixing the code is half the job. The other half is deciding how to re-run safely, which is the next section.

A dbt build is not one big transaction. Each node commits on its own, so when something fails halfway, some work is already done and stays done. That makes one question central: is running it again safe? For most work, yes. Tables and views are replaced, incremental merges on a unique key merge, and grants are simply applied again. But append models, and hooks that insert rows, are not. Run them twice and you store their rows twice. We had an on run end hook that wrote an audit row. It ran at the end of the failed build, and again at the end of dbt retry, so the audit table now shows two rows for what was really one run. The second trap is rollback. A bad filter deployed, ran with a green OK, and emptied fct orders. We reverted the code in git, and the table stayed empty, because reverting code does not touch data. Only rebuilding the model from the reverted code restored the rows. So before re-running anything, ask whether any step wrote outside dbt's own tables, through hooks, operations or calls to other systems, because none of that rolls back. And design every step to be safe to repeat, and keep a list of the ones that are not.

One bad row can stop an incremental model, and nothing will tell you. Someone loaded a test payment dated in the year two thousand thirty. The incremental model picked it up, and its watermark, the maximum paid at, jumped to twenty thirty. The loader then deleted the test row, but the incremental table kept it, and kept the watermark with it. Two real payments arrived in October. Neither was newer than twenty thirty, so both were skipped. After that run, the table held eight payments totalling forty, while the source held nine totalling fifty nine. And every run reported OK. The recovery has three steps. First, delete the bogus row from the table. Second, backfill a bounded window: the model reads a backfill from variable, and re-reads everything since the first of October, merging what is already there. Third, reconcile: nine rows and fifty nine on both sides. Fourth, rebuild everything downstream of the repaired model, so the fix reaches the marts. To prevent it happening again, add a test on the watermark column itself: no paid at may lie in the future.

Everything underneath your project keeps moving: packages, the adapter, and the engine itself. Each upgrade can change what actually runs. Here is a real package upgrade. dbt utils version one removed the old surrogate key macro. A project still calling it fails to compile, and the message carries a warning worth reading: the replacement treats null values differently to empty strings. So switching macros can change the keys themselves, and anything joined on them. The safe pattern is the same for every kind of upgrade. Change one thing at a time, in its own pull request. Read deprecation warnings while they are still warnings, before a later release turns them into errors, like the arguments warning on generic tests in course four. Compile the project before and after the upgrade, and diff the compiled folder, so you see every line of SQL that changed. Then run CI, and compare row counts and totals. Pinning makes all of this deliberate. The dbt core and adapter pins, and the package lock file, mean nothing moves until you decide to move it, and that is when you read the release notes. The engine is the biggest upgrade of all. Moving from one point twelve to dbt version two is an engine change, so treat it as one: clear the deprecations first, then run a full CI build.

A performance regression passes every test, because tests check rows, not time. Only timing shows it. Here is a real one. A single change to dim customers took it from four hundredths of a second to forty two hundredths: nearly ten times slower. The build said OK, and every test passed. Nothing would have flagged it, except a comparison of timings. That comparison is simple to set up. Keep each production run's run results file. After every run, compare each model's execution time with the previous run, and sort by the ratio between them. Look at the biggest ratios first, not the biggest totals, because a model that suddenly takes ten times longer is news, while a model that has always been slow is not. On Snowflake, credits follow running time, so a model that is ten times slower is roughly ten times the cost. Snowflake's query history shows the same thing per query, across every tool that uses the warehouse, not only dbt. Finally, when the warehouse is busy, prioritise. Run the critical marts first, or on a warehouse of their own, and let everything else wait its turn.

Incidents go better when the steps are written down before anyone needs them. A good runbook has five. First, tell consumers, starting with the owner named in the exposure, so nobody acts on a wrong number while you work. Second, read the state: the artefacts, the logs, and the tables themselves, as in the diagnosis section. Third, choose a repair for what you actually found: a retry for a failed run, a bounded backfill for a missed window, a full refresh only when the source still holds everything. Fourth, reconcile totals against the source, because a repair is just another claim until the numbers agree. Fifth, write it up: the cause, the fix, and the new check that would have caught it sooner. Keep the evidence, too. Production manifests and run results, the freshness files, the logs and the audit table, kept for as long as you might need to explain a number. And one thing must never be lost. Snapshots hold history that exists nowhere else. Next, the final course: one shared meaning for revenue.

In September, the sales dashboard reported revenue of fifty nine. The finance pack reported twenty five. Both teams were confident, and both queries were correct. The problem was never the SQL. It was the definition. Each report wrote its own sum, and one counted refunded and unpaid orders while the other did not. A metric fixes this by defining revenue exactly once. It lives in YAML, next to the models: a measure, the sum of order amounts, plus the filter Finance agreed, completed and shipped orders only, written into the metric itself, with a description saying who agreed it. Querying it with MetricFlow returned thirteen for the first of September and twelve for the third: twenty five in total, Finance's number.
