From now on, any tool that asks for revenue gets the same rule, instead of rewriting it. A metric does not fix everything, though. If the mart underneath is wrong, every report is now wrong in exactly the same way, and the definition still needs a named owner who can change it. Be clear, too, about where this runs. MetricFlow is open source, and we queried it locally against our own warehouse. Serving metrics to BI tools through the hosted Semantic Layer is a separate service, so check its eligibility for your plan before relying on it.

A semantic model describes a mart in the terms that metrics need, and it has three parts. Entities are the keys. In the orders model, order is the primary entity, one per row, and customer is a foreign entity, pointing at the customers model. Dimensions are what you group and filter by, such as status and order date. Measures are what you aggregate, such as the sum of amount. Joins then follow the entities, and only in the safe direction. Asking for revenue by customer country joined many orders to one customer each: a many-to-one join, which cannot duplicate rows. It returned three for the UK, ten for Germany and twelve for France. Now the protection. We defined a customer count and asked for it by order status, which needs a one-to-many join, exactly the fan-out from course three. MetricFlow refused, saying there was no valid join path. But notice what the metric inherits. Ana's September order counts under Germany, because dim customers holds her current country. A metric is only as right as the mart underneath it.

Step back and look at the shop's revenue product as a whole, from the loader to the dashboard. At every layer there was an alternative, and it is worth saying why we chose what we did. For modelling, we chose staging then marts, rather than one wide table, so raw data has exactly one entry point. For persistence, views for staging and tables for marts, with an incremental model only where history is large enough to matter. For history, a snapshot of customers, because the source overwrites countries. For orchestration, the command line under your own orchestrator, so nothing is locked to a single vendor. And for the metric, a single definition, so that reports cannot drift apart. None of these is the answer. Each one was chosen for stated requirements: how much data there is, how late it arrives, who is on the team, and what the budget allows. Change a requirement, and the right choice may change with it. So when you present a design, start with its requirements. Then every choice reads as a consequence, and can be challenged on its own terms.

Six months from now, someone will ask why fct payments is incremental, and the person who decided may have moved on. Write the answer down now, as an architecture decision record. A good record is short. Context and decision, in a line or two each. The evidence, which here is real: the late payment that a maximum timestamp filter missed and the lookback caught, and the append run that doubled the rows. The consequences, including what was given up, such as deletes that the incremental model never sees, and new columns that are not backfilled, so the team runs a weekly full refresh and reconciles after every run. And finally, the condition for revisiting it: if lateness grows beyond three days, or the table becomes cheap enough to rebuild. Migrating fct payments from a table to an incremental model changes how it is built, not what it promises consumers. So reconcile its rows against a full rebuild, keep its columns, types and name unchanged, and tell the owners listed in the exposures. Keep these records in the repository, reviewed like code.

You can now explain a dbt project from end to end: how it compiles, what it builds in the warehouse, how it is tested and documented, how it is deployed through review, and how it is repaired when something goes wrong. Be honest about what that means. This course explained. It did not assess you, and following worked examples is not the same as being responsible for production. That needs demonstrated practice. Build the shop project on a warehouse of your own. Get real pull requests reviewed by the people who own the numbers. And run an incident, even a rehearsed one: diagnose it, repair it, reconcile the totals, and write it up. Some topics were left out on purpose: ingestion tools, warehouse administration, custom adapters and materializations, the hosted Semantic Layer and multi-project features, and dbt version two. Each has its own documentation, and each deserves its own study. Finally, keep current. Pin your versions, read the release notes when you move them, and check every claim, including the ones in this course, against the engine you actually run.
